Most injuries were mild (66%, p<0.001). Muscular (40.9%) and ligamentous (37.4%) injuries were
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            the most common injury types. Fractures and ligamentous injuries were significantly more severe than muscular and other injuries (P<0.05).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            even though week 17 had the highest mean number of shoulder injuries at 10.75/season, there was no apparent shoulder injury distribution trend
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            across the football season.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONCLUSIONS: Shoulder injuries are common in American football. Introducing a deidentified injury registry that provides detailed injury
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            information in the Nfl may help develop better prevention strategies and protocols.

18	     Purpose: To investigate the inﬂuence of shorter, more frequent rest breaks with per-cooling as an alternative heat-acclimation session
19	     on physiological, perceptual, and self-paced maximal cycling performance, compared with continuous heat exposure. Methods:
20	     Thirteen participants completed 1 continuous and 3 intermittent-heat-exposure (IHE) maximal self-paced cycling protocols in a
21	     random order in heat (36 °C, 80% relative humidity): 1 × 60-minute exercise (CON), 3 × 20-minute exercise with 7.5-minute rest
22	     between sets (IHE-20), 4 × 15-minute exercise with 5-minute rest between sets (IHE-15), and 6 × 10-minute exercise with 3-minute
23	     rest between sets (IHE-10). Mixed-method per-cooling (crushed-ice ingestion and cooling vest) was applied during rest periods of all
24	     IHE protocols. Results: Total distance completed was greater in IHE-10, IHE-15, and IHE-20 than in CON (+11%, +9%, and +8%,
25	     respectively), with no difference observed between IHE protocols. Total time spent above 38.5 °C core temperature was longer in
26	     CON compared with IHE-15 and IHE-20 (+62% and +78%, respectively) but similar to IHE-10 (+5%). Furthermore, a longer time
27	     above 38.5 °C core temperature occurred in IHE-10 versus IHE-15 and IHE-20 (+54% and +69%, respectively). Sweat loss did not
28	     differ between conditions. Conclusion: IHE with per-cooling may be a viable alternative heat-acclimation protocol in situations
29	     where training quality takes precedence over thermal stimulus or when both factors hold equal priority.

   Single Session Intermittent Heat Exposure With More Frequent
  and Shorter Cooling Breaks Facilitates Greater Training Intensity
  and Elicits Physiological Responses Comparable to Continuous
                           Heat Exposure
Julian A.P. Ramos,1 Kagan J. Ducker,1 Hugh Riddell,1 Grant Landers,2 Olivier Girard,2 and Carly J. Brade1
                1
                    Curtin School of Allied Health, Curtin University, Bentley, WA, Australia; 2School of Human Sciences (Exercise and Sport Science),
                                                            University of Western Australia, Perth, WA, Australia

     Purpose: To investigate the inﬂuence of shorter, more frequent rest breaks with per-cooling as an alternative heat-acclimation session
     on physiological, perceptual, and self-paced maximal cycling performance, compared with continuous heat exposure. Methods:
     Thirteen participants completed 1 continuous and 3 intermittent-heat-exposure (IHE) maximal self-paced cycling protocols in a
     random order in heat (36 °C, 80% relative humidity): 1 × 60-minute exercise (CON), 3 × 20-minute exercise with 7.5-minute rest
     between sets (IHE-20), 4 × 15-minute exercise with 5-minute rest between sets (IHE-15), and 6 × 10-minute exercise with 3-minute
     rest between sets (IHE-10). Mixed-method per-cooling (crushed-ice ingestion and cooling vest) was applied during rest periods of all
     IHE protocols. Results: Total distance completed was greater in IHE-10, IHE-15, and IHE-20 than in CON (+11%, +9%, and +8%,
     respectively), with no difference observed between IHE protocols. Total time spent above 38.5 °C core temperature was longer in
     CON compared with IHE-15 and IHE-20 (+62% and +78%, respectively) but similar to IHE-10 (+5%). Furthermore, a longer time
     above 38.5 °C core temperature occurred in IHE-10 versus IHE-15 and IHE-20 (+54% and +69%, respectively). Sweat loss did not
     differ between conditions. Conclusion: IHE with per-cooling may be a viable alternative heat-acclimation protocol in situations
     where training quality takes precedence over thermal stimulus or when both factors hold equal priority.

     Keywords: heat acclimation, self-paced, cycling

1

*Address for correspondence:

                                               2
 Abstract
A vegan diet is associated with reduced cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, but protein

deficiencies may be detrimental to skeletal muscle structure and function. The aim of this

study was to compare the vascular and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy,

recreationally active habitual vegan (VEG) and omnivorous (OMN) men. Sixteen OMN and

nine VEG underwent ultrasound scans to determine brachial artery flow-mediated dilation

(FMD) and carotid artery intima-media thickness (cIMT) and vastus lateralis (VL) muscle

thickness and fascicle pennation angle. Knee extension maximal voluntary isometric

contraction (MVIC) force was assessed on an isokinetic dynamometer, and 𝑉̇ O2max on a cycle

ergometer and online gas analysis system. A three-day food diary determined habitual dietary

behaviour. Bayesian analyses of independent groups provided ‘moderate’ to ‘very strong’

evidence for lower consumption of absolute (63±21 g/d vs. 98±30 g/d; Bayes Factor

(BF01)=0.140) and relative (0.86±0.29 g/kg/d vs. 1.36±0.52 g/kg/d; BF01=0.259) protein,

absolute saturated fat (15.2±7.9 g vs. 30.3±11.8 g; BF01=0.089) and cholesterol (5.0±6.0 mg

vs. 337.9±232.6 mg; BF01=0.019) in VEG compared to OMN, respectively. Further, there

was ‘anecdotal’ evidence to support no differences in FMD (3.37±3.31% vs. 4.58±5.82%;

BF01=2.591), cIMT (0.51±0.07mm vs. 0.49±0.04mm; BF01=2.510), VL thickness

(26.1±3.7mm vs. 27.8±6.4mm; BF01=2.726), fascicle pennation angle (16.6±4.7° vs.

17.7±3.7°; BF01=2.844), MVIC (627±182 N vs. 551±102 N; BF01=1.656) or 𝑉̇ O2max

(40.8±9.8 ml/kg/min vs. 35.8±5.2 ml/kg/min; BF01=1.218) between VEG and OMN,

respectively. Despite marked differences in habitual nutrient intake, healthy, young vegan

and omnivorous men did not differ regarding vascular and skeletal muscle structure and

function, or cardiovascular fitness.




Key words: diet, skeletal muscle, ultrasonography, endothelium, vascular

                                                                                          3
 Introduction
Epidemiological studies suggest that plant-based diets, characterised by a high consumption

of whole grains, fruits and vegetables, are typically associated with a reduced risk of

cardiovascular disease incidence and mortality compared to omnivorous diets (Kim et al.,

2019). However, less is known about the effect plant-based diets have on specific skeletal

muscle and vascular characteristics that are associated with long-term health conditions.

Ultrasound measurements of carotid artery intima-media thickness (cIMT) and endothelial

function assessed via flow-mediated dilation (FMD) are commonly used surrogate markers of

atherosclerotic development and cardiovascular disease risk (Kokubo et al., 2018; Matsuzawa

et al., 2015). Healthy elderly vegetarian men and women have been shown to exhibit higher

brachial artery FMD compared with omnivores (Lin et al., 2001) albeit with a suboptimal

measurement approach for FMD (Thijssen et al., 2019). More recently, research has

demonstrated lower cIMT in young healthy vegetarian men compared with their omnivorous

counterparts (Acosta-Navarro et al., 2017). To our knowledge there is only one study that has

investigated the effects of a vegan diet on the vasculature, indicating that microvascular

function did not improve following just four weeks compliance to a vegan diet (Rogerson et

al., 2018). Consequently, it is unclear whether a habitual vegan diet confers any direct

benefits to vascular structure or function.

Despite the purported health benefits, there are potential risks of nutrient deficiencies

associated with vegan diets. Protein intake, for example, is lower in vegan dieters compared

with omnivores, and in some cases less than the minimum recommended daily protein intake

(Sobiecki et al., 2016). Protein consumption increases postprandial myofibrillar protein

synthesis (MPS) rates (Tipton et al., 1999), subsequently contributing to muscle mass

accretion (Hartman et al., 2007). Given that muscle mass is the main determinant of

maximum strength (Jones et al., 1989), it is plausible that lower protein consumption in

                                                                                            4
 vegan diets could be associated with (smaller and therefore) weaker muscles (Sahni et al.,

2015). However, previous studies have demonstrated no differences in upper and lower body

one-repetition maximum (1-RM) (Boutros et al., 2020), or knee extensor isokinetic peak

torque between young physically active vegan/vegetarian and omnivorous women (Lynch et

al., 2016) Nonetheless, as participants were highly trained, it is not clear how training status

and the interaction with diet may have impacted these findings. It should also be noted that

no prior studies have included assessment of muscle morphology or architecture. Skeletal

muscle architecture (including thickness and fascicle pennation angle) are key determinants

of the maximum force of a muscle (Aagaard et al., 2001), therefore assessment of muscle

architecture in habitual, untrained vegan and omnivorous dieters may confirm existing

evidence suggesting similarities in maximal muscle strength.

Despite the potential disadvantages of plant-based diets for strength/power performance,

evidence suggests no differences exist in maximal power output during an incremental

cycling bout between vegans, lacto-ovovegetarians and omnivores (Nebl et al., 2019).

Contrarily, there is some evidence that 𝑉̇ O2max is higher in female elite vegetarian vs.

omnivore endurance athletes (Lynch et al., 2016). Further, highly physically active (150-200

minutes of moderate intensity physical activity/week) vegan females exhibit a greater

estimated 𝑉̇ O2max when compared with omnivores (Boutros et al., 2020). However,

estimating rather than measuring 𝑉̇ O2max is problematic and both studies used highly trained

populations, which limits the application of the study findings. For example, chronic

endurance (McPhee et al., 2009) and resistance (Erskine et al., 2011; Erskine et al., 2010)

exercise, as well as ageing (Janssen et al., 2000) induce physiological adaptations that will

likely confound any measurable effect of diet on vascular or muscle properties.

To date, no study has combined ultrasound assessments of vascular structure and function

with skeletal muscle architecture, as well as maximal force and measured 𝑉̇ O2max, in habitual
                                                                                              5

and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy, untrained men who were either

habitual vegan or omnivorous dieters. We hypothesised that vegan dieters would have higher

FMD and 𝑉̇ O2max, but lower cIMT values compared with omnivorous dieters, whereas

omnivores would have larger and stronger knee extensor muscles.

Methods
Twenty-five young, healthy men with no history of resistance or endurance exercise training

in the preceding six months were recruited for the current study, which was a single-centre,

cross-sectional design. Participant characteristics are shown in Table 1. Further exclusion

criteria included smokers, those with a history of lower limb injuries in the six months prior

to testing and those engaging in more than two hours per week of structured exercise.

14	     Postexercise hydration is fundamental to replace ﬂuid loss from sweat. This study evaluated rehydration and gastrointestinal (GI)
15	     symptoms for each of three beverages: water (W), sports drink (SD), and skimmed, lactose-free milk (SLM) after moderate-
16	     intensity cycling in the heat. Sixteen college students completed three exercise sessions each to lose ≈2% of their body mass.
17	     They drank 150% of body mass loss of the drink assigned in randomized order; net ﬂuid balance, diuresis, and GI symptoms were
18	     measured and followed up for 3 hr after completion of ﬂuid intake. SLM showed higher ﬂuid retention (∼69%) versus W (∼40%;
19	     p < .001); SD (∼56%) was not different from SLM or W (p > .05). Net ﬂuid balance was higher for SLM (−0.26 kg) and SD
20	     (−0.42 kg) than W (−0.67 kg) after 3 hr (p < .001), resulting from a signiﬁcantly lower diuresis with SLM. Reported GI
21	     disturbances were mild and showed no difference among drinks (p > .05) despite ingestion of W (1,992 ± 425 ml), SD
22	     (1,999 ± 429 ml), and SLM (1,993 ± 426 ml) in 90 min. In conclusion, SLM was more effective than W for postexercise
23	     rehydration, showing greater ﬂuid retention for the 3-hr follow-up and presenting with low-intensity GI symptoms similar to
24	     those with W and SD. These results conﬁrm that SLM is an effective option for hydration after exercise in the heat.

  Skimmed, Lactose-Free Milk Ingestion Postexercise: Rehydration
   Effectiveness and Gastrointestinal Disturbances Versus Water
           and a Sports Drink in Physically Active People
                 Luis F. Aragón-Vargas, Julián C. Garzón-Mosquera, and Johnny A. Montoya-Arroyo
                        Human Movement Science Research Center (CIMOHU-UCR), University of Costa Rica (UCR), San Jose, Costa Rica

     Postexercise hydration is fundamental to replace ﬂuid loss from sweat. This study evaluated rehydration and gastrointestinal (GI)
     symptoms for each of three beverages: water (W), sports drink (SD), and skimmed, lactose-free milk (SLM) after moderate-
     intensity cycling in the heat. Sixteen college students completed three exercise sessions each to lose ≈2% of their body mass.
     They drank 150% of body mass loss of the drink assigned in randomized order; net ﬂuid balance, diuresis, and GI symptoms were
     measured and followed up for 3 hr after completion of ﬂuid intake. SLM showed higher ﬂuid retention (∼69%) versus W (∼40%;
     p < .001); SD (∼56%) was not different from SLM or W (p > .05). Net ﬂuid balance was higher for SLM (−0.26 kg) and SD
     (−0.42 kg) than W (−0.67 kg) after 3 hr (p < .001), resulting from a signiﬁcantly lower diuresis with SLM. Reported GI
     disturbances were mild and showed no difference among drinks (p > .05) despite ingestion of W (1,992 ± 425 ml), SD
     (1,999 ± 429 ml), and SLM (1,993 ± 426 ml) in 90 min. In conclusion, SLM was more effective than W for postexercise
     rehydration, showing greater ﬂuid retention for the 3-hr follow-up and presenting with low-intensity GI symptoms similar to
     those with W and SD. These results conﬁrm that SLM is an effective option for hydration after exercise in the heat.

     Keywords: hydration, acute GI problems, ﬂuid balance, dairy

9	                              LUETKEMEIER, M. J., J. M. HANISKO, and K. M. AHO. Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and Na+ Concentration. Med. Sci. Sports
10	                              Exerc., Vol. 49, No. 7, pp. 1432–1436, 2017. The popularity of tattoos has increased tremendously in the last 10 yr particularly among
11	                              athletes and military personnel. The tattooing process involves permanently depositing ink under the skin at a similar depth as eccrine sweat
12	                              glands (3–5 mm). Purpose: The purpose of this study was to compare the sweat rate and sweat Na+ concentration of tattooed versus
13	                              nontattooed skin. Methods: The participants were 10 healthy men (age = 21 T 1 yr), all with a unilateral tattoo covering a circular area at
14	                              least 5.2 cm2. Sweat was stimulated by iontophoresis using agar gel disks impregnated with 0.5% pilocarpine nitrate. The nontattooed
15	                              skin was located contralateral to the position of the tattooed skin. The disks used to collect sweat were composed of TygonÒ tubing
16	                              wound into a spiral so that the sweat was pulled into the tubing by capillary action. The sweat rate was determined by weighing the disk
17	                              before and after sweat collection. The sweat Na+ concentration was determined by flame photometry. Results: The mean sweat rate from
18	                              tattooed skin was significantly less than nontattooed skin (0.18 T 0.15 vs 0.35 T 0.25 mgIcmj2Iminj1; P = 0.001). All 10 participants
19	                              generated less sweat from tattooed skin than nontattooed skin and the effect size was j0.79. The mean sweat Na+ concentration from
20	                              tattooed skin was significantly higher than nontattooed skin (69.1 T 28.9 vs 42.6 T 15.2 mmolILj1; P = 0.02). Nine of 10 participants had
21	                              higher sweat Na+ concentration from tattooed skin than nontattooed skin, and the effect size was 1.01. Conclusions: Tattooed skin
22	                              generated less sweat and a higher Na+ concentration than nontattooed skin when stimulated by pilocarpine iontophoresis. Key Words:

                                                                                             ABSTRACT
                              LUETKEMEIER, M. J., J. M. HANISKO, and K. M. AHO. Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and Na+ Concentration. Med. Sci. Sports
                              Exerc., Vol. 49, No. 7, pp. 1432–1436, 2017. The popularity of tattoos has increased tremendously in the last 10 yr particularly among
                              athletes and military personnel. The tattooing process involves permanently depositing ink under the skin at a similar depth as eccrine sweat
                              glands (3–5 mm). Purpose: The purpose of this study was to compare the sweat rate and sweat Na+ concentration of tattooed versus
                              nontattooed skin. Methods: The participants were 10 healthy men (age = 21 T 1 yr), all with a unilateral tattoo covering a circular area at
                              least 5.2 cm2. Sweat was stimulated by iontophoresis using agar gel disks impregnated with 0.5% pilocarpine nitrate. The nontattooed
                              skin was located contralateral to the position of the tattooed skin. The disks used to collect sweat were composed of TygonÒ tubing
                              wound into a spiral so that the sweat was pulled into the tubing by capillary action. The sweat rate was determined by weighing the disk
                              before and after sweat collection. The sweat Na+ concentration was determined by flame photometry. Results: The mean sweat rate from
                              tattooed skin was significantly less than nontattooed skin (0.18 T 0.15 vs 0.35 T 0.25 mgIcmj2Iminj1; P = 0.001). All 10 participants
                              generated less sweat from tattooed skin than nontattooed skin and the effect size was j0.79. The mean sweat Na+ concentration from
                              tattooed skin was significantly higher than nontattooed skin (69.1 T 28.9 vs 42.6 T 15.2 mmolILj1; P = 0.02). Nine of 10 participants had
                              higher sweat Na+ concentration from tattooed skin than nontattooed skin, and the effect size was 1.01. Conclusions: Tattooed skin
                              generated less sweat and a higher Na+ concentration than nontattooed skin when stimulated by pilocarpine iontophoresis. Key Words:
                              PILOCARPINE, IONTOPHORESIS, HYPOHIDROSIS, DERMIS, ECCRINE GLAND

Isokinetic testing

Isokinetic strength testing (System 3, Biodex, New York, USA) was performed on three separate
occasions: 1) during the annual periodic health evaluation (both limbs) pre-injury, 2) during the
C
initial examination within seven days post-injury (contralateral uninjured limb only), and 3) prior
to the final RTS assessment (both limbs).
C
Prior to isokinetic testing, the athletes were instructed as to the nature and purpose of the
isokinetic testing. They performed a standardized warm-up procedure comprising five minutes
A
on a stationary exercise bike (Technogym, Italy) at a resistance (in W) equivalent to 1.5 times
their bodyweight (in kg) at their chosen cadence (typically this was approximately 85 rpm). Prior
to each isokinetic test, the athlete was instructed as to the mode of testing, and given a minimum
of three practice repetitions, and testing was not started unless the athlete thought they were
ready to do so. For the periodic health evaluation, the order (i.e. left, right) was randomized, and

Testing comprised three modes and speeds. First, the players were tested over five repetitions of

D

DISCUSSION
In this series of 41 professional soccer players with an MRI-confirmed hamstring injury, novel
analyses, comparing isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS to pre-injury strength
measures, are presented, as well as between-limb comparisons. The present results suggest that a
10% difference (positive or negative) is present in a large proportion of players at RTS following
hamstring injury, and the distribution of isokinetic strength variables in the injured limb at RTS
are similar to pre-injury strength measures. Additionally, the side-to-side strength differences
are similar at RTS when compared to pre-injury strength differences.
 Return to sport decision making after hamstring injury
Only one previous study has investigated isokinetic strength at RTS, suggesting that restoration
of isokinetic strength (compared to the uninjured limb) does not seem to be required for the
successful completion of a criteria based rehabilitation program.(17) However, this comparison
was made between limbs, comparing the injured to the uninjured side. The present study is the
first to compare RTS strength to pre-injury strength in the same limb.
Making RTS decisions following hamstring injuries is challenging. Different criteria have been
suggested, but there is a lack of validated criteria and poor consensus on which measurements
are useful to determine readiness to RTS.(9) Although evidence to support a specific
recommendation is lacking, a cut-off of 10% compared to the uninjured side continues to be
prevalent in research studies and clinical practice.(13) However, the present results suggest that a
10% difference (positive or negative) is present in a large proportion of players at RTS following
hamstring injury and is even observed in a similar proportion of players pre-injury.
Regardless of statistical significance, the small changes in the isokinetic measures and large
confidence intervals suggest that it would be clinically meaningless to impose a specific cut-off
value as a criterion for RTS (figure 2). Furthermore, it is clear from figure 3C that a large
percentage of players displayed strength changes in the injured limb at RTS compared to pre-
injury strength for all the isokinetic variables. The side-to-side differences observed pre-injury
and at RTS (figure 3A and 3B) are similar to the change in the injured limb (figure 3C), apart
from a greater percentage of players demonstrating a >20% difference at RTS. It remains
difficult to determine which isokinetic strength cut-offs are useful to determine when players are
ready for RTS, or indeed, which players are at greater risk of re-injury.
 Risk of re-injury
Risk of re-injury is considered a potential decision modifier,(7) with recurrent injuries typically
reported to occur early after RTS.(25–28) Isokinetic strength differences with specific cut-offs
are thought to identify players at greater risk of re-injury, and therefore promoted as a criterion
not only in RTS,(29) but also when used to determine progression during a criteria-based
rehabilitation program.(12) As the second trial from which we included players is still ongoing,
we were unable to investigate re-injury data, and only one of the players from the completed trial
suffered a re-injury within the first two months.
However, a previous investigation in the same cohort as this present study (53.7% of the players
in the current study were also included in the previous analysis) reported no differences in
isokinetic strength at RTS between those players who experienced hamstring re-injury, and those
who did not.(17) A recent randomized trial among recreational athletes, comparing early and
delayed rehabilitation, also found no difference in isokinetic strength at RTS, reporting just one
re-injury for the entire cohort.(30) These findings(17,30) suggest that isokinetic strength may not
need to be fully restored to limit re-injury risk if a criteria-based rehabilitation program is
completed successfully.
Isokinetic strength differences
Isokinetic side-to-side strength differences at RTS are commonly presented as deficits.(11,17,29)
This may reflect a bias in our view of strength profiles, as strength is preferentially reported as
what is “missing”, i.e. the injured leg being weaker. However, as demonstrated in figure 4, a
similarly large proportion of players present with a positive strength difference, i.e. the injured
leg being stronger. Thus, approximately 60% of the players had at least one negative or positive
 isokinetic hamstring strength difference of more than 10%. Strength differences, whether
positive or negative, seem to be a standard finding for isokinetic dynamometry testing, and so-
called “deficits” should be interpreted with caution.
There were no significant differences in strength of the uninjured limb for any of the isokinetic
modes of testing pre-injury compared to the post-injury tests during the initial assessment (figure
2). Although we observe a slight decrease in strength in the uninjured limb post-injury, the
reason for this is not known. Quadriceps and hamstrings concentric strength at 60°/s
demonstrated a statistically significant change in the injured limb (table 2) between RTS and pre-
injury strength, but the small absolute differences are well within the minimal detectable change
values for these modes of isokinetic testing.(29) Together with the large confidence intervals,
these small differences indicate little clinical value in this finding.
Variability
The asymmetries presented may form useful reference data for clinicians. Importantly, these data
should be interpreted in light of the variability within isokinetic testing that has been previously
documented.(29) In figure 3 and 4, where we compare the strength at RTS to pre-injury, as well
as side-to-side differences, the 95% CI includes 50% of the population for any of the varying
cut-points from 5% to 20%.
If we consider that the minimal detectable change in peak torque for all these measures is greater
than 20%,(19) it is apparent that the previously suggested 10% cut-point is likely overly
conservative; beyond the capability of the measurement due to a large amount of intra-individual
variability. Recently, we have also shown that isokinetic strength varies by 15% from one pre-
season to the next.(31) If we were to compare the pre-injury and RTS strength, these results
 would need to be interpreted in light of the substantial variability we might expect within
individual players over time.
It seems that 20% is more likely a reasonable „cut-point‟ for when an isokinetic strength
difference represents a true difference, however, this cut-off requires further investigation as a
potential risk factor. The use of isokinetic testing in isolation is not supported, and can at best
only be considered a component in RTS decision making.(32)
Strengths and limitations
A major strength of this study is that all tests performed utilized the same isokinetic testing
system with highly experienced assessors, and it was performed in a single clinical setting for
professional athletes. All players underwent standardized criteria-based rehabilitation protocols,
together with a standardized and comprehensive RTS assessment. The hamstring injuries
included were confirmed with both clinical examinations and positive MRI results. However,
since only grade I and II injuries were included, it remains unknown if our results can be
extrapolated to MRI negative or grade III (complete avulsions) hamstring injuries.
The isokinetic dynamometry strength testing was performed at the end of the final soccer
specific training session as part of the RTS assessment. Therefore, players may have been
somewhat fatigued at the time of testing, and it is not known whether this may have influenced
the results. Although the isokinetic test results were not used as a set criterion in the RTS
decision, the sports medicine physician were not blinded to the results. Since we could not
control the weighting and influence of every bit of information used in the process, we cannot be
sure how the isokinetic results, or indeed a number of other factors, may have influenced the
RTS decision.
 An important limitation in this study is incomplete re-injury data. Although only one re-injury
was registered from the completed trial, we do not know the re-injury rate in the second trial.
This study was performed in a multinational, multi-language setting, and while every effort was
made to guarantee that players comprehended the test procedure and directions, it is possible that
some players did not fully understand the instructions. We also acknowledge the homogeneity of
our study population of professional male soccer players, which limits the generalization of these
findings to other sports, age groups or female players.
Clinical implications
The use of isokinetic strength testing in isolation as a criterion for RTS is not supported by these
data. Importantly, side-to-side isokinetic strength differences are common at RTS, and when
compared to pre-injury strength. The injured limb presents with similar strength differences
when comparing strength at RTS to pre-injury measures, and in a large proportion of players it
might favor the injured limb. The previous accepted cut-off of 10% is inappropriate, as side-to-
side strength differences of 5-20% are commonly found, both at RTS and pre-injury.
CONCLUSION     C
The distribution of positive and negative isokinetic strength differences when comparing strength
at RTS to pre-injury measures were similar, urging clinical caution when interpreting these
results. Small changes in isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS compared to pre-injury
strength suggest that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful to guide restoration of strength as a
criterion for RTS after hamstring injury.

Isokinetic strength testing (System 3, Biodex, New York, USA) was performed on three separate
occasions: 1) during the annual periodic health evaluation (both limbs) pre-injury, 2) during the
C
initial examination within seven days post-injury (contralateral uninjured limb only), and 3) prior
to the final RTS assessment (both limbs).
C
Prior to isokinetic testing, the athletes were instructed as to the nature and purpose of the
isokinetic testing. They performed a standardized warm-up procedure comprising five minutes
A
on a stationary exercise bike (Technogym, Italy) at a resistance (in W) equivalent to 1.5 times
their bodyweight (in kg) at their chosen cadence (typically this was approximately 85 rpm). Prior
to each isokinetic test, the athlete was instructed as to the mode of testing, and given a minimum
of three practice repetitions, and testing was not started unless the athlete thought they were
ready to do so. For the periodic health evaluation, the order (i.e. left, right) was randomized, and

DISCUSSION
In this series of 41 professional soccer players with an MRI-confirmed hamstring injury, novel
analyses, comparing isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS to pre-injury strength
measures, are presented, as well as between-limb comparisons. The present results suggest that a
10% difference (positive or negative) is present in a large proportion of players at RTS following
hamstring injury, and the distribution of isokinetic strength variables in the injured limb at RTS
are similar to pre-injury strength measures. Additionally, the side-to-side strength differences
are similar at RTS when compared to pre-injury strength differences.
 Return to sport decision making after hamstring injury
Only one previous study has investigated isokinetic strength at RTS, suggesting that restoration
of isokinetic strength (compared to the uninjured limb) does not seem to be required for the
successful completion of a criteria based rehabilitation program.(17) However, this comparison
was made between limbs, comparing the injured to the uninjured side. The present study is the
first to compare RTS strength to pre-injury strength in the same limb.
Making RTS decisions following hamstring injuries is challenging. Different criteria have been
suggested, but there is a lack of validated criteria and poor consensus on which measurements
are useful to determine readiness to RTS.(9) Although evidence to support a specific
recommendation is lacking, a cut-off of 10% compared to the uninjured side continues to be
prevalent in research studies and clinical practice.(13) However, the present results suggest that a
10% difference (positive or negative) is present in a large proportion of players at RTS following
hamstring injury and is even observed in a similar proportion of players pre-injury.
Regardless of statistical significance, the small changes in the isokinetic measures and large
confidence intervals suggest that it would be clinically meaningless to impose a specific cut-off
value as a criterion for RTS (figure 2). Furthermore, it is clear from figure 3C that a large
percentage of players displayed strength changes in the injured limb at RTS compared to pre-
injury strength for all the isokinetic variables. The side-to-side differences observed pre-injury
and at RTS (figure 3A and 3B) are similar to the change in the injured limb (figure 3C), apart
from a greater percentage of players demonstrating a >20% difference at RTS. It remains
difficult to determine which isokinetic strength cut-offs are useful to determine when players are
ready for RTS, or indeed, which players are at greater risk of re-injury.
 Risk of re-injury
Risk of re-injury is considered a potential decision modifier,(7) with recurrent injuries typically
reported to occur early after RTS.(25–28) Isokinetic strength differences with specific cut-offs
are thought to identify players at greater risk of re-injury, and therefore promoted as a criterion
not only in RTS,(29) but also when used to determine progression during a criteria-based
rehabilitation program.(12) As the second trial from which we included players is still ongoing,
we were unable to investigate re-injury data, and only one of the players from the completed trial
suffered a re-injury within the first two months.
However, a previous investigation in the same cohort as this present study (53.7% of the players
in the current study were also included in the previous analysis) reported no differences in
isokinetic strength at RTS between those players who experienced hamstring re-injury, and those
who did not.(17) A recent randomized trial among recreational athletes, comparing early and
delayed rehabilitation, also found no difference in isokinetic strength at RTS, reporting just one
re-injury for the entire cohort.(30) These findings(17,30) suggest that isokinetic strength may not
need to be fully restored to limit re-injury risk if a criteria-based rehabilitation program is
completed successfully.
Isokinetic strength differences
Isokinetic side-to-side strength differences at RTS are commonly presented as deficits.(11,17,29)
This may reflect a bias in our view of strength profiles, as strength is preferentially reported as
what is “missing”, i.e. the injured leg being weaker. However, as demonstrated in figure 4, a
similarly large proportion of players present with a positive strength difference, i.e. the injured
leg being stronger. Thus, approximately 60% of the players had at least one negative or positive
 isokinetic hamstring strength difference of more than 10%. Strength differences, whether
positive or negative, seem to be a standard finding for isokinetic dynamometry testing, and so-
called “deficits” should be interpreted with caution.
There were no significant differences in strength of the uninjured limb for any of the isokinetic
modes of testing pre-injury compared to the post-injury tests during the initial assessment (figure
2). Although we observe a slight decrease in strength in the uninjured limb post-injury, the
reason for this is not known. Quadriceps and hamstrings concentric strength at 60°/s
demonstrated a statistically significant change in the injured limb (table 2) between RTS and pre-
injury strength, but the small absolute differences are well within the minimal detectable change
values for these modes of isokinetic testing.(29) Together with the large confidence intervals,
these small differences indicate little clinical value in this finding.
Variability
The asymmetries presented may form useful reference data for clinicians. Importantly, these data
should be interpreted in light of the variability within isokinetic testing that has been previously
documented.(29) In figure 3 and 4, where we compare the strength at RTS to pre-injury, as well
as side-to-side differences, the 95% CI includes 50% of the population for any of the varying
cut-points from 5% to 20%.
If we consider that the minimal detectable change in peak torque for all these measures is greater
than 20%,(19) it is apparent that the previously suggested 10% cut-point is likely overly
conservative; beyond the capability of the measurement due to a large amount of intra-individual
variability. Recently, we have also shown that isokinetic strength varies by 15% from one pre-
season to the next.(31) If we were to compare the pre-injury and RTS strength, these results
 would need to be interpreted in light of the substantial variability we might expect within
individual players over time.
It seems that 20% is more likely a reasonable „cut-point‟ for when an isokinetic strength
difference represents a true difference, however, this cut-off requires further investigation as a
potential risk factor. The use of isokinetic testing in isolation is not supported, and can at best
only be considered a component in RTS decision making.(32)
Strengths and limitations
A major strength of this study is that all tests performed utilized the same isokinetic testing
system with highly experienced assessors, and it was performed in a single clinical setting for
professional athletes. All players underwent standardized criteria-based rehabilitation protocols,
together with a standardized and comprehensive RTS assessment. The hamstring injuries
included were confirmed with both clinical examinations and positive MRI results. However,
since only grade I and II injuries were included, it remains unknown if our results can be
extrapolated to MRI negative or grade III (complete avulsions) hamstring injuries.
The isokinetic dynamometry strength testing was performed at the end of the final soccer
specific training session as part of the RTS assessment. Therefore, players may have been
somewhat fatigued at the time of testing, and it is not known whether this may have influenced
the results. Although the isokinetic test results were not used as a set criterion in the RTS
decision, the sports medicine physician were not blinded to the results. Since we could not
control the weighting and influence of every bit of information used in the process, we cannot be
sure how the isokinetic results, or indeed a number of other factors, may have influenced the
RTS decision.
 An important limitation in this study is incomplete re-injury data. Although only one re-injury
was registered from the completed trial, we do not know the re-injury rate in the second trial.
This study was performed in a multinational, multi-language setting, and while every effort was
made to guarantee that players comprehended the test procedure and directions, it is possible that
some players did not fully understand the instructions. We also acknowledge the homogeneity of
our study population of professional male soccer players, which limits the generalization of these
findings to other sports, age groups or female players.
Clinical implications
The use of isokinetic strength testing in isolation as a criterion for RTS is not supported by these
data. Importantly, side-to-side isokinetic strength differences are common at RTS, and when
compared to pre-injury strength. The injured limb presents with similar strength differences
when comparing strength at RTS to pre-injury measures, and in a large proportion of players it
might favor the injured limb. The previous accepted cut-off of 10% is inappropriate, as side-to-
side strength differences of 5-20% are commonly found, both at RTS and pre-injury.
CONCLUSION     C
The distribution of positive and negative isokinetic strength differences when comparing strength
at RTS to pre-injury measures were similar, urging clinical caution when interpreting these
results. Small changes in isokinetic strength of the injured limb at RTS compared to pre-injury
strength suggest that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful to guide restoration of strength as a
criterion for RTS after hamstring injury.

  "abstract": "Injury data from the 2019 to 2022 NFL seasons were extracted from the official NFL injury report and secondary sources.   "methods": "Descriptive epidemiological study of NFL injury reports for the 2019 to 2022 seasons, with shoulder injuries classified by type and severity (games missed). Injury rates were calculated per 1000 athletic exposures using a one-game-per-athlete rule, and playoff games were excluded. Positions were compared with ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis and t-tests.",

Muscular/tendinous injuries were 40.9% (185) and ligamentous injuries 37.4% (169), and fractures were 1.3% (6). Fractures and ligamentous injuries were significantly more severe than muscular/tendinous and other injuries, and week 17 had the highest mean count with no overall seasonal trend.",
  "limitations": "The data came from media and public compilations, which may contain reporting discrepancies and vague injury labels. Only the 2019 to 2022 seasons were included, the design is descriptive and cannot show causes, and yearly counts differ slightly between tables (2020 appears as 129, 130 and 131 across the text and tables).",
  "practicalImplications": "Shoulder injuries are common in NFL players and mostly mild, but they still cost games on average. The authors suggest rotator cuff strengthening, gradual training-load progression, proper equipment fit and a deidentified injury registry to guide prevention.",
  "athleteDev": "Position-specific shoulder work may suit linebackers, cornerbacks and wide receivers, who had the highest shoulder injury counts, with gradual load progression as the authors suggest.   "rtp": "This study cannot guide return-to-play decisions because it reports injury counts and games missed, not recovery criteria, rehabilitation or re-injury outcomes."

 "sports": ["Soccer"],

 "evidenceSummary": "Pooled analysis of 41 professional male soccer players with an MRI-confirmed hamstring injury, drawn from two single-site randomized trials at Aspetar in Qatar. Isokinetic strength of the injured limb at return to sport was compared with each player's own pre-injury screening values, and side-to-side differences were compared at both time points. The injured limb averaged over 95% of pre-injury strength, with 63.4% of players showing a >10% deficit and 57.9% a >10% surplus in at least one of five variables at return to sport, similar to pre-injury patterns.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This observational pooled analysis covers 41 players from one clinical setting, includes only grade I and II injuries, and has incomplete re-injury data, so it cannot test whether isokinetic cut-offs predict re-injury. Results may not apply to other sports, female players or MRI-negative injuries.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 10% deficit figure as proof that many players are still weak at return, but similar proportions also differ from their own pre-injury values, and the authors argue these differences fall within test variability.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2019,
  "citation": "van Dyk N, Wangensteen A, Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, Bahr R, Tol J, et al. Similar Isokinetic Strength Preinjury and at Return to Sport after Hamstring Injury. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000001900",
  "abstract": "The study compared isokinetic strength of the injured hamstring at return to sport with pre-injury screening values in 41 professional male soccer players with MRI-positive hamstring injury. Injured-limb strength at return to sport averaged over 95% of pre-injury strength, and side-to-side differences were similar at return to sport and pre-injury. The authors conclude that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful for guiding strength restoration as a return-to-sport criterion.",
  "tldr": "Hamstring-injured professional soccer players were about as strong at return to sport as before injury, and a 10% side-to-side cut-off did not separate players well. Isokinetic cut-offs should not be used alone to clear players to return.",
  "methods": "Pooled data from two single-site randomized trials, including 41 players with MRI-positive hamstring injury who had pre-injury isokinetic screening. Concentric knee flexion and extension were tested pre-injury, within seven days of injury (uninjured limb only) and before the return-to-sport assessment, at 60 and 300 degrees per second.",
  "findings": "Injured-limb strength at return to sport averaged above 95% of pre-injury strength. The proportions with a >10% difference were similar at return to sport and pre-injury, and the only statistically significant change (quadriceps and hamstring concentric strength at 60 degrees per second) was small and within the minimal detectable change.",
  "limitations": "Testing was done at the end of a training session, so players may have been fatigued, and physicians were not blinded to the isokinetic results. Only grade I and II injuries were included, re-injury data are incomplete (one re-injury in the completed trial), and the population was homogeneous professional male soccer players. The abstract reports the strength values, and the discussion frames the 20% cut-point as needing further study.",
  "practicalImplications": "Isokinetic strength should not be used alone as a return-to-play criterion or against a fixed 10% cut-off. Expect both deficits and surpluses in the injured leg at return, and read them against the athlete's own pre-injury profile where it exists.",
  "athleteDev": "This study cannot guide training choices for performance. Its use is limited to reading strength testing, where the athlete's own pre-injury baseline is the better reference than the uninjured side.",
  "rtp": "Supports keeping isokinetic testing as one part of return-to-sport decisions, not a stand-alone criterion. It did not link strength at return to re-injury risk, because the re-injury data were incomplete."
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id": "Q52",
 "sourceFile": "Single nucleotide polymorphisms and tendon-ligament injuries in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms and Tendon/Ligament Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Healthy Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 31 studies (1,687 injured and 2,227 control athletes) of genetic variants and tendon or ligament injury across several sports, with a meta-analysis of 12 studies covering four variants. Only the VEGFA rs699947 C allele was associated with a lower injury risk (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.98, p = 0.03, I2 = 3.82%), and COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722 and MMP3 rs679620 showed no significant association.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The VEGFA estimate pools only four studies (408 cases, 395 controls), and most included studies are small candidate-gene designs, so the associations are not causal. The conclusions say heterogeneity was confirmed, while the reported I2 for VEGFA is low, so the pooled result needs cautious reading.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read VEGFA rs699947 as a usable genetic marker for tendon and ligament injury risk, but it is one borderline association from four studies and cannot be used to screen or select athletes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Fukuyama Y, Murakami H, Iemitsu M. Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms and Tendon/Ligament Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Int J Sports Med. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1055/a-2419-4359",
  "abstract": "The review aimed to identify associations between genetic polymorphisms and tendon and ligament injuries in adolescent and adult athletes of multiple sports. It included 31 articles (1,687 injury cases and 2,227 controls) and identified 144 candidate polymorphisms, and the meta-analysis of 12 articles covered COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722, MMP3 rs679620 and VEGFA rs699947. Only VEGFA rs699947 was associated with injury, with the C allele linked to a lower risk (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.98).",
  "tldr": "One gene variant (VEGFA rs699947, C allele) was linked to about 20% lower tendon and ligament injury risk in athletes, based on four studies. The other candidate variants showed no clear link, so genetic screening for these injuries is not supported yet.",
  "methods": "Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, Cochrane Library and MEDLINE to 7 July 2023 for genetic association studies of tendon or ligament injury in athletes. Study quality was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and pooled odds ratios used DerSimonian and Laird random-effects models.",
  "findings": "Of 144 candidate polymorphisms in 31 studies, four were pooled. For VEGFA rs699947, the C allele versus A allele gave OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.98, p = 0.03, I2 = 3.82%), while the dominant and recessive models were not significant. COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722 and MMP3 rs679620 showed no significant effect in any genetic model.",
  "limitations": "The VEGFA finding rests on four studies, and few candidate-gene studies met meta-analysis criteria. The mechanisms of several variants are unclear, many studies came from one region so ethnic comparisons are limited, and competitive level, training time and nutrition were not accounted for.",
  "practicalImplications": "Genetic variants are not yet usable to identify athletes at risk of tendon or ligament injury. The VEGFA result needs replication in larger samples before any practical use.",
  "athleteDev": "This review cannot inform athlete development or training choices, since it covers injury association only. Genotype-based selection or program design is not supported by these findings.",
  "rtp": "Cannot guide return to sport: the review compares injured and uninjured athletes and gives no information on rehabilitation, recovery or return timelines."
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id": "Q54",
 "sourceFile": "Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise - Rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances vs water and a sports drink in physically active people.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Skimmed, Lactose-Free Milk Ingestion Postexercise: Rehydration Effectiveness and Gastrointestinal Disturbances Versus Water and a Sports Drink in Physically Active People' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized crossover study in which 16 physically active college students (4 women, 12 men) lost about 2% of body mass cycling in a heat chamber at 32 degrees C, then drank 150% of the loss over 90 minutes of water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk, with follow-up for 3 hours. Fluid retention was about 70% with milk and 40% with water (p < .001), with the sports drink at about 56%, not significantly different from either; mild gastrointestinal symptoms did not differ among drinks.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample was 16 physically active students rather than athletes, tested once per drink after a single 2% dehydration, with 3 hours of follow-up. Milk did not differ significantly from the sports drink on fluid retention, and gastrointestinal symptoms were self-rated on questionnaires.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read milk as superior to sports drinks for rehydration, but milk outperformed water, while milk and the sports drink did not differ significantly.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Aragón-Vargas LF, Garzón-Mosquera JC, Montoya-Arroyo JA. Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise: rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances versus water and a sports drink in physically active people. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijsnem.2023-0253",
  "abstract": "This study compared rehydration after moderate-intensity cycling in the heat with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk in 16 physically active college students, measuring net fluid balance, diuresis and gastrointestinal symptoms over 3 hours. Milk showed higher fluid retention (about 69%) than water (about 40%), and the sports drink (about 56%) did not differ from either. Gastrointestinal symptoms were mild and did not differ among drinks.",
  "tldr": "After a 2% body-mass loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk retained more fluid than water over 3 hours, with mild gut symptoms similar to the other drinks. It was not significantly different from a sports drink on fluid retention.",
  "methods": "Randomized crossover design in which 16 physically active college students each completed three sessions of cycling in a heat chamber (32 degrees C, 70% relative humidity) to lose about 2% of body mass. They then drank 150% of the loss in three aliquots over 90 minutes, with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk, and fluid balance, urine output and gastrointestinal symptoms were measured for 3 hours.",
  "findings": "Fluid retention was about 69.8% for milk, 55.6% for the sports drink and 39.6% for water. Net fluid balance at 3 hours was -0.26 kg for milk, -0.42 kg for the sports drink and -0.67 kg for water, and the milk-water contrast was significant (-0.40 kg). Gastrointestinal symptom scores were low and did not differ among conditions.",
  "limitations": "The sample was small and recreationally active rather than trained athletes, and the study tested one heat exposure with about 2 L of fluid. The milk-sports drink difference was not significant for retention or net fluid balance, and the abstract's comparison of sports drink with milk on net balance rests on the same non-significant contrast noted in the results.",
  "practicalImplications": "After a moderate sweat loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk may be a practical option for rehydration when it is tolerated, as it retained more fluid than water. A sports drink performed in between, so choice can rest on tolerance and preference.",
  "athleteDev": "For athletes rehydrating after training in the heat, milk gave better fluid retention than water in this study, so it is a reasonable option if the athlete tolerates it. The study did not test carbohydrate or electrolyte goals, so it does not settle drink choice for performance needs.",
  "rtp": "Cannot inform return to sport: the participants were physically active students without injury, and the study measured only post-exercise hydration."
 }
}

== Q50 results ==
“quadriceps” (knee extension) and “hamstring” (knee flexion) muscles. Finally, players
performed five repetitions of eccentric knee extension at 60°/s which measured the eccentric
strength of the knee flexors (principally the “hamstring” muscles). The reliability of the
isokinetic tests has been described previously.(19)
Standardized rehabilitation protocols
The participants in both randomized control trials completed comparable standardized criteria-
based rehabilitation protocols. The protocols included range of motion exercises, progressive
strengthening exercises and an incremental, progressive return to running program. The
rehabilitation was performed at one location, supervised by one of six sports physical therapists
with 7–25 years of experience treating athletes. The (treating) physiotherapist was blinded to the
MRI findings. In both trials functional, criteria-based progressions (as opposed to time-based
progressions) were utilized for the six-stage rehabilitation protocols.(17,23) The rehabilitation
protocol for the first study has been published,(17) and the structure of the two different
protocols       used        in      the
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fzex_zG1JtA;
second        trial      is      freely       available       online:
http://www.aspetar.com/AspetarFILEUPLOAD/UploadCenter/636209313253275549_Aspetar%
20Hamstring%20Protocol.pdf )
 Soccer-specific training
After successfully finishing the first three stages of the rehabilitation protocol, the final stages of
soccer-specific training were supervised by a sports rehabilitator with more than 10 years of
experience in professional soccer. The protocol consisted of three stages (typically completed in
three days) and progression of volume and intensity of direction changes, sprints, jumps, passes,
shooting, interval running, one-on-one attacking and defending drills. The training was designed
to mimic muscle fatigue and competitiveness during soccer training and game situations.
Successful completion of the soccer-specific training was defined as full sports-specific
functional ability without obvious limitations and/or symptoms.(17)
Return to sport
The player had to complete the soccer-specific training before the RTS assessment was
performed. The treating sports medicine physician was informed of the physical therapists‟ RTS
assessment findings, which included clinical examinations, as well as any comments from the
sports rehabilitator regarding the on-field sessions. With this information (from the physical
therapist and sports rehabilitator), the sports medicine physician then took a history, performed a
clinical examination, and then decided on the athlete‟s readiness to RTS. RTS was defined as the
number of days between initial injury and return to full unrestricted training and/or match
play.(17) Acute hamstring strain injuries at the same site that occurred within 2 months from
RTS, were classified as re-injuries.(4,24)
Statistical analyses
All statistical analyses were performed with Excel 2016 (Microsoft, Redmond, USA) and SPSS
software (V.20.0; SPSS, Chicago, Illinois, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean
with standard deviation (SD). We analyzed differences in binomial data between groups with an
 unpaired t test. Significance was assumed if the p value was less than 0.05. The percentage was
calculated of players with 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% isokinetic strength difference when
comparing 1) the contralateral limbs pre-injury, 2) the contralateral limbs at RTS, and 3) the
ipsilateral limb pre-injury to RTS.
RESULTS
The inclusion of players into the study is outlined in figure 1. In total, 41 soccer players (age 25
± 4 yrs, height 175 ± 6 cm, body mass 71 ± 7 kg, body mass index 23 ± 2 kg/m2) were included.
There was no significant difference in any of these measures between the 72 excluded players
(age 24 ± 5 yrs, height 177 ± 6 cm, weight 73 ± 9 kg, body mass index [BMI] 23 ± 2 kg/m2) and
the 41 players included (p >0.05).
Of the 41 injuries, 21 were classified as grade I injuries and 20 as grade II, with 73.1% located in
the biceps femoris long head, 22.0% in the semimembranosus, and 4.9% in the semitendinosus.
The injured players included six forwards, 17 midfielders, 17 defenders, and one goalkeeper. The
players included in this analysis took on average 25.3 ± 8.9 days to RTS. One player suffered a
re-injury from the completed trial.
The isokinetic strength of the players pre-injury during the periodic health evaluation (both
limbs), post-injury at initial assessment (uninjured limb only), and at RTS (both limbs) is
presented in figure 2, demonstrating only small changes in strength between the measurements.
Quadriceps and hamstrings concentric strength at 60°/s demonstrated statistically significant
differences of 4.9% and 5.3% respectively when comparing the injured limb at RTS to pre-injury
(table 2).
 At RTS, the average strength of the injured limbs was >95% normalized to the pre-injury
strength for all measurements (table 2). The side-to-side differences in isokinetic strength are
presented as percentages for isokinetic strength pre-injury (panel A) and at RTS (panel B). The
same cut-offs are used when comparing the change in strength at RTS to pre-injury in the injured
limb (panel C); figure 3 demonstrating a negative difference (i.e. the injured leg was weaker) and
figure 4 a positive difference (i.e. the injured leg was stronger). The greatest difference (non-
significant with large CIs) was found for the cut-offs of >20% when comparing panel C to panels
A and B (figure 3).
Overall, 63.4% of the players had a >10% negative side-to-side strength difference (i.e. injured
limb being weaker) and 57.9% of the players had a >10% positive strength difference (i.e.
injured limb being stronger) in at least one of the five isokinetic variables (figures 3 and 4).
DISCUSSION

Of the 41 injuries, 21 were classified as grade I injuries and 20 as grade II, with 73.1% located in
the biceps femoris long head, 22.0% in the semimembranosus, and 4.9% in the semitendinosus.
The injured players included six forwards, 17 midfielders, 17 defenders, and one goalkeeper. The
players included in this analysis took on average 25.3 ± 8.9 days to RTS. One player suffered a
re-injury from the completed trial.
The isokinetic strength of the players pre-injury during the periodic health evaluation (both
limbs), post-injury at initial assessment (uninjured limb only), and at RTS (both limbs) is
presented in figure 2, demonstrating only small changes in strength between the measurements.
Quadriceps and hamstrings concentric strength at 60°/s demonstrated statistically significant
differences of 4.9% and 5.3% respectively when comparing the injured limb at RTS to pre-injury
(table 2).
 At RTS, the average strength of the injured limbs was >95% normalized to the pre-injury
strength for all measurements (table 2). The side-to-side differences in isokinetic strength are
presented as percentages for isokinetic strength pre-injury (panel A) and at RTS (panel B). The
same cut-offs are used when comparing the change in strength at RTS to pre-injury in the injured
limb (panel C); figure 3 demonstrating a negative difference (i.e. the injured leg was weaker) and
figure 4 a positive difference (i.e. the injured leg was stronger). The greatest difference (non-
significant with large CIs) was found for the cut-offs of >20% when comparing panel C to panels
A and B (figure 3).
Overall, 63.4% of the players had a >10% negative side-to-side strength difference (i.e. injured
limb being weaker) and 57.9% of the players had a >10% positive strength difference (i.e.
injured limb being stronger) in at least one of the five isokinetic variables (figures 3 and 4).

 "sourceFile": "Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and        Na+ Concentration.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",

 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and Na+ Concentration' (Luetkemeier, Hanisko, Aho, Med Sci Sports Exerc 2017) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "low",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Within-person laboratory study of 10 apparently healthy young men, each with a tattoo covering at least 5.2 cm2 on one side of the body and untattooed skin on the other. Sweat was induced at rest by pilocarpine iontophoresis, with sweat rate and sweat sodium measured from each site. Sweat rate was about half as high from tattooed skin (0.18 vs 0.35 mg/cm2/min, p = 0.001), and sweat Na+ was higher (69.1 vs 42.6 mmol/L, p = 0.02), with nine of ten men showing the higher sodium on the tattooed side.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Ten healthy non-athlete men were tested at rest with no exercise or heat load, so the study cannot show effects on heat tolerance or hydration during training. The authors call the findings preliminary, the mechanism is unknown, and the link to athletes is background rather than tested.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as proof that tattooed athletes sweat less and lose more sodium in training heat, but the study used resting pilocarpine stimulation with no heat or exercise, so it cannot support any change to hydration or heat plans.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2017,
  "citation": "Luetkemeier MJ, Hanisko JM, Aho KM. Skin tattoos alter sweat rate and Na+ concentration. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017;49(7):1432-1436.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000001244",
  "abstract": "The study compared sweat rate and sweat Na+ concentration from tattooed and nontattooed skin in 10 healthy men, using pilocarpine iontophoresis. Tattooed skin produced less sweat (0.18 vs 0.35 mg/cm2/min) and sweat with more sodium (69.1 vs 42.6 mmol/L) than nontattooed skin. The authors conclude that tattooed skin altered sweat function, and the changes did not relate to tattoo age.",
  "tldr": "Tattooed skin sweated about half as much as untattooed skin and gave sweat with higher sodium when stimulated at rest. Whether this changes sweat loss or heat tolerance during exercise has not been tested.",
  "methods": "Within-person comparison in 10 apparently healthy men with a tattoo of at least 5.2 cm2 on one side of the body and untattooed skin at the contralateral site. Sweat was stimulated by two 5-minute cycles of pilocarpine iontophoresis, collected for 20 minutes on a sweat collection disk, and analyzed for rate (by weight) and sodium (by flame photometry). Tattooed and nontattooed sites were compared with paired t-tests, and tattoo age was correlated with the ratios.",
  "findings": "Sweat rate from tattooed skin was 0.18 +/- 0.15 vs 0.35 +/- 0.25 mg/cm2/min for nontattooed skin (p = 0.001), with all 10 men sweating less on the tattooed side (ratio 0.53). Sweat Na+ was 69.1 +/- 28.9 vs 42.6 +/- 15.2 mmol/L (p = 0.02), with nine of ten men higher on the tattooed side. Tattoo age explained less than 1% of the variance in the sweat rate ratio and about 6% of the sodium ratio.",
  "limitations": "The sample was 10 men, the stimulus was pilocarpine at rest in a room controlled at 19 to 21 C, and no heat load or exercise was applied. The authors state the mechanism is unclear, that the results are preliminary, and that it is unknown whether similar changes occur with heat stress or internal heat production.",
  "practicalImplications": "Under pilocarpine stimulation at rest, tattooed skin produced less sweat with a higher sodium concentration, so heavily tattooed athletes may warrant attention in hot conditions. This has not been tested during exercise or heat stress, so it should not change current hydration plans yet.",
  "athleteDev": "This study does not give a performance or training prescription. It suggests tattooed skin may sweat differently, which could matter for heat-training planning, but that needs testing during exercise before it informs practice.",
  "rtp": "Cannot inform return to sport: participants were healthy non-athletes with no injury, and the study measured sweat function at rest only."
 }
}
